bodies.intuition: Merging two models degrades both a little. Merging eight degrades all of them a lot. The reason is that the fine-tunes do not agree about what to do with the same weights — one wants a coordinate raised, another wants it lowered — and averaging splits the difference in a way that satisfies neither.
bodies.engineer: The mitigations all attack the same thing from different angles. Trim each task vector to its largest-magnitude coordinates, since most of a fine-tune's displacement is noise. Resolve sign conflicts by majority before averaging, so opposing directions do not cancel to nothing. Drop a large random fraction of the vector and rescale the rest, which works surprisingly well and is evidence for how redundant these displacements are.
bodies.math: Interference grows with the number of models merged because the chance that any given coordinate is contested rises with each one added. If each task vector touches a fraction of coordinates, the expected number of contested coordinates grows roughly with the square of the model count while the useful signal grows only linearly — so there is a count past which adding a model makes the merge worse, and it arrives sooner than the linear intuition suggests.
